exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Diagonal Matrix

question.text: For the matrix $ A= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}, $ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
question.explanation:
For an "almost" zero $m \times n$ matrix with non-zero entries

\[ \sigma_1, \: \sigma_2, \: \ldots, \: \sigma_r \]

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n \times m$ matrix with entries

\[ {\sigma_1^{-1}}, \, {\sigma_2^{-1}}, \, \ldots, \, {\sigma_r^{-1}} \]

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} A^+ &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\\ 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}^+ \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4^{-1} &\!\!\! 0 &0 \\ \!\!0 &\, 2^{-1} &0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 &0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Pseudoinverse of a Matrix Given Its Singular Value Decomposition

question.text: \[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} {2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
question.explanation:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

\[ V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T, \]

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$

First, notice that

\[ V = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma^+ = \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad U^T = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A^+ &= V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ U =\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1} {\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1} {\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
question.explanation:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

\[ V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T, \]

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$

First, notice that

\[ V = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma^+ = \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad U^T = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A^+ &= V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
question.explanation:
If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

\[ V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T, \]

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$

First, notice that

\[ V = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma^+ = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad U^T = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A^+ &= V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{20} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\- 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{20} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{20} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

If $A=U \Sigma V ^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

\[ V \, \Sigma^+ \, U^T, \]

where $\Sigma^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma.$

First, notice that

\[ V = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma^+ = \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad U^T = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: \[ U_r = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{4}{5} \\ \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma_r = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V_r = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse $A^+.$
question.explanation:
If $A=U_r \Sigma_r V_r ^T$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

\[ V_r \, \Sigma_r^+ \, U_r^T, \]

where $\Sigma_r^+$ is the pseudoinverse of $\Sigma_r.$

First, notice that

\[ \Sigma_r^+ = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad U_r^T = \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we have

\begin{align*} A^+ &= V_r \, \Sigma_r^+ \, U_r^T \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{25} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 &0 &0 \end{bmatrix} . \end{align*}
